exercises.title: List documents with filters
exercises.summary: Build a list query that supports keyword search, owner filtering, and stable ordering.
exercises.problemStatement: Your document service needs a `list documents` endpoint. Return only active documents, support an optional owner filter, and preserve deterministic ordering so the mobile client can paginate safely.
acceptanceCriteria: The optional owner filter narrows the result set.
Results are ordered by updated time descending.

taskSteps.title: Start from the base query
taskSteps.description: Limit the source to active documents before adding optional filters.

taskSteps.title: Apply the optional owner filter
taskSteps.description: Handle the filter only when a value is supplied.

taskSteps.title: Stabilize ordering
taskSteps.description: Sort consistently so the same page request gives the same order.

hints.concept: This is a classic list endpoint: filter, sort, then project to a lightweight DTO.
hints.structure: Keep a base query, branch on the optional owner filter, then apply ordering before materializing.
hints.pseudocode: Start from documents where `IsArchived == false`, add `Where` for owner when needed, then `OrderByDescending` by update time.
hints.lineHint: In C#, think `var query = documents.Where(x => !x.IsArchived); if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(owner)) query = query.Where(...);`
hints.fullExplain: A passing solution needs filtering, deterministic sorting, and one projected list result.

reflectionPrompts: Why should ordering be explicit on list endpoints even when the data source looks stable?
How would you add cursor pagination later without rewriting the whole method?

requirements.label: Filters archived rows
requirements.feedback: Filter out archived rows before returning documents.

requirements.label: Applies owner filter
requirements.feedback: Apply the owner filter when a value is provided.

starterFiles.main.py:
rows = [
    {"title": "Architecture Notes", "owner": "Nina", "is_archived": False, "updated_at": 1700},
    {"title": "Quarterly Report", "owner": "Nina", "is_archived": False, "updated_at": 2000},
    {"title": "Retired Draft", "owner": "Nina", "is_archived": True, "updated_at": 2100},
    {"title": "Spec", "owner": "Minh", "is_archived": False, "updated_at": 1800},
]

for item in list_active(rows, "Nina"):
    print(f"{item['title']}:{item['updated_at']}")

exercises.title: Project document cards with LINQ
exercises.summary: Use LINQ to transform document rows into compact card DTOs for the mobile home screen.
exercises.problemStatement: Convert raw document rows into light card objects that keep only the title, owner, and a concise status label. Use a single LINQ pipeline so the shape is easy to reason about.
acceptanceCriteria: Uses LINQ for filtering or projection.
Projects into a lighter response shape.
Keeps the owner and status information.

hints.concept: This is a projection problem: keep only the fields the UI needs.
hints.structure: Filter the active rows, then project to card DTOs with `Select`.
hints.lineHint: Look for `Where` plus `Select` in the same chain.
hints.fullExplain: A compact LINQ projection is enough to pass.

reflectionPrompts: When should the API return a lighter DTO instead of the full entity?
What makes a LINQ pipeline easier to debug later?

requirements.label: Uses Select
requirements.feedback: Project rows into a card model with `Select`.

exercises.title: Protect a transaction aggregate
exercises.summary: Enforce aggregate invariants so a transfer cannot settle twice.
exercises.problemStatement: Your transaction service has a transfer aggregate that can be authorized, settled, and cancelled. Add domain methods so a settled transfer cannot be settled twice and a cancelled transfer cannot move forward again.
acceptanceCriteria: Explicit domain methods gate state changes.

hints.concept: The aggregate should own its state machine instead of leaving it to controllers.
hints.structure: Add methods like `Authorize`, `Settle`, and `Cancel` with guard clauses.
hints.pseudocode: Before changing status, check the current status and throw for invalid transitions.
hints.lineHint: Guard clauses plus a `Status` enum are enough.
hints.fullExplain: Passing means the aggregate blocks double-settlement and post-cancel settlement.

reflectionPrompts: Why do aggregates own transition rules instead of letting handlers toggle fields directly?
How would you persist an audit trail without weakening the aggregate boundary?

exercises.title: Protect the dispatch inbox from race conditions
exercises.summary: Use synchronization to ensure two workers cannot claim the same message twice.
exercises.problemStatement: Two background workers are competing to claim work from the same in-memory inbox. Add coordination so the same message cannot be claimed twice, even when both workers check at the same time.
acceptanceCriteria: Shared state changes happen inside one critical section.
A claimed message cannot be claimed again.
The approach remains easy to explain to the next maintainer.

hints.concept: This is a shared-state timing issue, so you need one small critical section around the claim step.
hints.structure: Check and update the inbox status while holding the same lock.
hints.pseudocode: Inside the lock: find pending message, mark it claimed, return it.
hints.fullExplain: Passing means no second worker can observe the same message as still pending after the first one claims it.

reflectionPrompts: Why is idempotency still useful even after you add locking?
What would change if the inbox moved from memory into a database table?

requirements.label: Uses locking
requirements.feedback: Protect the claim path with an explicit synchronization primitive.

starterFiles.main.py:
from inbox import Inbox

inbox = Inbox()
print(inbox.claim_next())

exercises.title: Window a social feed query
exercises.summary: Build a timeline slice that returns only the newest posts for a specific author set.
exercises.problemStatement: A Twitter-like feed page needs the latest posts from a chosen set of authors. Filter by author ids, sort descending by publish time, and cap the results to the requested page size.
acceptanceCriteria: Filters by the requested author ids.
Caps the output to the requested size.

hints.concept: Think timeline windowing: filter first, sort second, then limit.
hints.structure: Apply author filter, order by publish time descending, then take the page size.
hints.pseudocode: Where author in ids -> OrderByDescending publishedAt -> Take(limit).
hints.lineHint: A deterministic feed window is enough for this exercise.
hints.fullExplain: Passing means the result set respects filter, order, and limit.

reflectionPrompts: What breaks if feed ordering is not deterministic?
When would you move from offset paging to cursor paging?

exercises.title: Build a frequency counter
exercises.summary: Count repeated values with a single pass map.
exercises.problemStatement: Write a helper that returns how many times each value appears in the input list.

hints.concept: This is the classic frequency counter pattern.
hints.structure: Initialize an empty map, then increment inside one loop.
hints.lineHint: One pass and one map are enough.
hints.fullExplain: The checker only needs to see the counting pattern.

reflectionPrompts: When does a frequency map beat sorting first?
What would change if the input stream were too large for memory?

requirements.label: Uses a map
requirements.feedback: Use a map structure to accumulate counts.

exercises.title: Append a node to a linked list
exercises.summary: Practice pointer updates without losing the existing tail reference.
exercises.problemStatement: Given the head of a singly linked list, append a new node to the end and return the original head.
acceptanceCriteria: Attaches a new node without breaking the chain.

hints.concept: Walk until the tail, then set its next pointer.
hints.structure: Handle `None` first, otherwise traverse while `current.next` exists.
hints.pseudocode: if head is None return Node(value); walk to tail; tail.next = Node(value); return head
hints.lineHint: Keep the original head reference unchanged.
hints.fullExplain: Passing means the append logic handles both empty and non-empty lists.

reflectionPrompts: Why is returning the original head important for callers?
What tradeoff would a tail pointer remove here?

requirements.label: Updates next pointer
requirements.feedback: Attach the new node through a next-pointer update.

starterFiles.main.py:
head = Node(1, Node(2))
result = append(head, 3)
while result:
    print(result.value)
    result = result.next

exercises.title: Merge overlapping intervals
exercises.summary: Sort the ranges and merge while the next start overlaps the current end.
exercises.problemStatement: Given a list of intervals, merge all overlapping intervals and return a condensed list.

hints.concept: Sort first so overlaps appear next to each other.
hints.structure: Seed the result with the first interval, then merge or append while scanning.
hints.pseudocode: sort intervals; for each interval compare to the last merged interval end
hints.lineHint: Update the last merged end with `max(last_end, current_end)`.
hints.fullExplain: Passing means correct sort + merge behavior.

reflectionPrompts: Why does sorting by start time make the merge invariant work?
What would change if intervals were streamed and could not all be sorted first?

requirements.label: Sorts intervals
requirements.feedback: Sort by interval start before merging.

testCases.label: Merges overlaps in C#

exercises.title: Minimum meeting rooms
exercises.summary: Track overlap count while separate start and end times move forward.
exercises.problemStatement: Given meeting intervals, return the minimum number of rooms required so that all meetings can happen without overlap conflicts.
acceptanceCriteria: Returns the minimum required room count.

hints.concept: You are counting maximum overlap, not building actual room objects.
hints.structure: Sort starts and ends separately, then walk both pointers.
hints.pseudocode: If next start is before next end, need another room; otherwise free one room.
hints.lineHint: Two sorted arrays and two indices are enough.
hints.fullExplain: Passing means computing peak overlap correctly.

reflectionPrompts: Why is peak overlap the same as minimum required rooms?
When would a min-heap be a clearer choice than two-pointer arrays?
